title: Different perspectives and shared purpose

content.content: Graham Stallwood, Chief Executive of the Planning Inspectorate, reflects on some of the questions currently being asked about appeals, local plans and how we are preparing for the demands ahead.
I recently joined Have We Got Planning News For You for a wide-ranging conversation about the work of the Planning Inspectorate.

We covered everything from appeal timetables and the choice between hearings and inquiries to the changes to written representations and the significant number of local plans we are expecting over the coming months.
They were challenging questions, but important ones.

Planning works best when organisations across the system are open about the pressures they face, listen to different perspectives and work together to find practical solutions. So, I wanted to reflect on some of the issues raised and explain how we're approaching them.
Getting the balance right on appeal timetables
I know there is concern in parts of the sector about the time being taken to schedule some appeal events.
Most events happen within the windows we're aiming for, but there are currently some hearings and inquiries being scheduled later than I would like.
There are several reasons behind that. Sometimes we need an inspector with specialist knowledge. There can also be complex circumstances involving the parties to an appeal.
We're also preparing for an exceptional amount of local plan work. We're expecting the equivalent of around two-and-a-half to three years' worth of local plans to be submitted in December.

We've recruited around 35 additional inspectors to help us meet that challenge. Those colleagues need to be properly trained and given experience of examinations before taking on cases themselves. That has required some of our experienced inspectors to support their development, with a short-term impact on the resource available elsewhere.
It is a challenge, and I don't want to underplay the effect that delays can have on people using our services. But we're building capacity so that we're better placed to meet the demands ahead.
Predictability shouldn't mean inflexibility
Another concern raised with me was whether the drive to decide appeals within predictable timescales can lead to hearing and inquiry dates being imposed too rigidly.

Government is clear about the importance of greater certainty and predictability in the planning system. That's important not only for appellants, but for local authorities, communities and everyone else affected by a proposal.
There will be occasions when there are good reasons to change an event date. Equally, there will be occasions when delaying it isn't justified. We make those judgements carefully and fairly.
We're looking at how we can develop a clearer, more shared understanding with the sector about how those situations should be approached.
There is a role for all of us here. If we want a quicker and more predictable system, the Inspectorate and the organisations and professionals working with us need to help make that possible.
Fairness sits at the heart of what we do
During the discussion, my weekend role as a grassroots football referee cropped up.

There are, perhaps surprisingly, some similarities. Whether you're on a football pitch or working within the planning system, people want to know they've been heard, that the rules have been applied consistently and that decisions have been reached fairly, even when they don't agree with the outcome.

For me, a fair process isn't simply one where everyone receives the same treatment. People's circumstances differ, and sometimes treating people differently is precisely what's needed to achieve fairness.
What matters is whether people can answer some fundamental questions positively:
Was I listened to? Was the decision-making transparent? Was I treated with respect?
Those principles are fundamental to the legitimacy of the Planning Inspectorate.
They matter whether we're considering a planning appeal, examining a local plan or dealing with one of the many other types of casework that come to us.
Choosing the right procedure for an appeal
We also discussed concerns about some cases being dealt with through hearings rather than inquiries.
The starting point for us isn't how large or valuable a development is. It is what an inspector needs to find out to reach their decision.

If the evidence can be properly assessed through written representations, an oral event shouldn't be necessary. Where evidence needs to be explored further, the inspector will consider whether a hearing or inquiry is the appropriate way to do that.
The important thing is matching the complexity of the case, the inspector's experience and the process.
That principle also applies to the new Part 1 written representations process.

Part 1 does not change the criteria for deciding whether an appeal needs a hearing or inquiry. Where an inspector needs a hearing or inquiry to properly test and understand the evidence, that remains available.
Quality is about much more than the outcome
One question I am regularly asked is whether we look at the proportion of appeals individual inspectors allow or dismiss.
We can see that information, but looking at an inspector's performance simply through an allowed or dismissed percentage would be far too simplistic.

Different types of casework can produce very different patterns. Multiple appeals on one site, enforcement cases and other specialist areas can quickly change the proportion of appeals an Inspector allows or dismisses.
What matters is the quality of the decision.
Our quality assurance therefore looks much more deeply at areas such as the reasoning behind decisions, the way issues have been addressed and the clarity and tone of our work.

I don't want inspectors worrying about whether their next decision will increase or decrease an allowance rate. I want them concentrating on making the right decision based on the evidence in front of them in a consistently timely way.
Preparing for what's ahead
The Planning Inspectorate's work extends much further than the planning appeals most people are familiar with.

We deal with more than 40 different types of casework, from planning and enforcement appeals and local plan examinations to nationally significant infrastructure projects, rights of way, compulsory purchase orders and a range of other applications and decisions.
That breadth means we constantly need to think about where our expertise and resources are needed most.
The forthcoming influx of local plans will undoubtedly be a challenge. But we've been preparing for it.

Our new inspectors come from a range of built-environment professions, and they're already gaining experience alongside established inspectors. That's important not only for the immediate challenge but for developing the capability we'll need in the years ahead.
Working together
One thing my career in planning has taught me is that no single organisation or profession can make the planning system work on its own.
Local authorities, applicants, communities, developers, planning professionals, government and the Planning Inspectorate all see the system from slightly different perspectives.

Understanding those perspectives doesn't mean we will always agree. But being curious about them, listening to concerns and being prepared to work across organisational and professional boundaries gives us a much better chance of improving the system.
We want a Planning Inspectorate that makes high-quality decisions, treats people fairly and provides greater certainty about how long processes will take.
Those objectives aren't alternatives.
The challenge for us, and for the wider planning sector, is delivering them together.
Graham Stallwood Chief Executive, Planning Inspectorate

description: Graham Stallwood, Chief Executive of the Planning Inspectorate, recently joined Have We Got Planning News For You to discuss appeal timetables, hearings versus inquiries, and the surge of local plans expected this December.

title: Our T Level Success Story

content.content: Happy National T Levels Week! Running from 19 to 23 October, it’s the perfect time to celebrate how these placements are bringing fresh energy to our teams. We are excited to share the Going Forward into Employment (GFIE) team’s recent experiences.
What is T Levels Week?
T Levels Week celebrates T Levels—two-year technical qualifications co-designed with employers to equip young people for skilled careers.
It brings together schools, colleges, employers, and students to highlight the value of technical education and share success stories from across the country.

Speaking of success stories, we have some fantastic news of our own to celebrate: one of our very own GFIE Team members has just been named a Regional Winner for The Outstanding T Level Ambassador of the Year Award 2026!
We are incredibly proud of their dedication to championing technical education and supporting the next generation of talent
What are T Levels?

While awareness is still growing—around 60% to 70% of students, parents, and employers remain unfamiliar with them—T Levels are two-year technical qualifications in England for 16-to-19-year-olds after GCSEs. Equivalent to three A Levels, they blend 80% classroom study with 20% hands-on industry placement, offering a practical path alongside traditional academic or apprenticeship options.
A recent report by Alan Milburn emphasised the importance of connecting schools with employers.
By offering placements across diverse regions and teams, we help ensure work experience is accessible based on drive and capability rather than personal connections.
Get Involved with T Levels
Whether you are looking to kickstart your career, support your child's future, or bring fresh talent into your team, T Levels offer an exciting path forward.
Find out more about how T Levels can work for you, visit GOV.UK T Levels and Amazing Apprenticeships

title: From Research to Recommendation: My Summer in DDaT at UKEF

content.content: Over the last few months, I had an opportunity to intern in the Data, Digital and Technology (DDaT) division in UK Export Finance. I began this role directly after finishing my degree in law, so I was excited to embark on this adventure in the civil service. I was unsure on whether coming from a non-technical background would make me feel wildly out of my depth. I assumed that delivering digital services in the public sector would require a great deal of specialised technical experience, so I was curious to see how the skills I developed throughout university could add value to projects.

From the outset of my internship, I was welcomed into a friendly team that made integrating into a new environment seamless! To settle in, I had many 1-1 meetings which gave me an opportunity to get to know everyone personally and provided an insight into their daily roles. The introductions helped broaden my understanding of DDaT and put to bed any worries I previously had about coming from a non-technical background.
After those first two weeks, I felt a lot more confident in possible future career choices, and excited to get involved in work impacting users across UKEF.
The Digital & Transformation Playbook

The development of the Digital & Transformation playbook was the main project I worked on during my internship. The project aimed to answer one simple question: How can information across DDaT’s professions be organised in a way that make sense to the diverse teams?

Currently, information is spread across multiple resources and internal sites, resulting in disjointed information and confusing access for users. These pain points underpin the rationale behind developing a playbook which was more connected and usable across teams. Before starting this internship, I thought I would be assisting on the sidelines, but I was grateful to be able to take full ownership of this project from research to prototype iteration. I started to feel less like an intern and more like a colleague in the team.
Through the duration of the project I:
Reflections

One of my biggest take aways from this experience was that understanding users is integral to the success of any digital service. When I first learnt about the playbook, I thought that reorganising information would be the challenge, however, through user research methods, I quickly realised that the greatest challenge is understanding how users navigate and understand information.

This insight made me realise that, contrary to my initial assumption, digital departments do involve a great deal of human interaction demonstrating the importance of empathy and understanding in informing service design.

Perhaps my greatest reflection of the internship was that growth and confidence come from being trusted. In my first week I would not have thought that I would be independently leading such a major project, especially in a digital space. From researching to iterating prototypes, I surprised myself with the work I was able to take ownership of.

I wouldn’t have been able to do this without my wonderful team that were so helpful and supportive. I am super grateful for my incredible line manager, Ben Johnson, who gave me the foundation of confidence I needed to achieve such amazing things over the internship. I am immensely thankful for the time and effort that the team so generously offered and following this internship I am excited about the possibility of pursuing a career in the Civil Service.
This experience was truly a once in a lifetime opportunity and I feel ever so privileged to have started the first leg of my career in UKEF.

title: Opening GOV.UK Wallet sandbox to digital verification services
authors: Nicola Betz, Head of Policy, Strategy & Engagement, GOV.UK One Login & GOV.UK Wallet
Melody Cooper-Yau, Head of Product, GOV.UK One Login & GOV.UK Wallet

content.content: The Government Digital Service (GDS) is inviting registered digital verification service (DVS) providers to join the GOV.UK Wallet sandbox. This will be the first time that private sector organisations can test their verifier technology in a closed test environment (the sandbox) with a test digital driving licence.

This is a significant moment in the development of the digital driving licence. It allows us to start testing how services offered by DVS providers will interact with government issued credentials in the GOV.UK Wallet, helping us to learn, improve and build confidence before we start to introduce the digital driving licence from next year.

DVS providers who are independently certified against government standards and are on the government’s DVS register can join the sandbox. The technology they provide will enable information from the digital driving licence to be shared securely with other organisations who will accept the digital driving licence, such as pubs, cinemas and supermarkets.

Our approach helps people use digital credentials with confidence, knowing they are sharing information through trusted providers. This will also help to support the wider use of trusted digital credentials in the future.
Responsible, safe and secure technology
As you would expect for a product that will in time be available to millions of people across the UK, we are building the digital driving licence in a responsible, safe and secure way.
Following on from our testing at the end of last year, GDS and the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA) have continued to design, build and test the product. This has included:

We have also been building on the work of the first credential for the GOV.UK Wallet, the digital Veteran Card. Like the Veteran Card, the digital driving licence is designed to be an alternative to the physical card, not a replacement for it.
The sandbox goes live

The sandbox gives registered DVS providers access to a collection of tools, including test credentials and test data, allowing them to experiment and build integrations in a safe environment that is separate from live user data and designed specifically for testing and learning.
Specifically, the sandbox allows DVS providers to:

This collaboration in the test environment enables learning on both sides. DVS providers gain an opportunity to prepare their own services, while government gains valuable insight into how the ecosystem will work in real life.
Working with industry to prepare for rollout
Many organisations will play a role in helping people use and verify digital credentials in the future. DVS providers are a key part of that.

Working closely with DVS providers helps us understand how digital credentials will operate in practice, are shared securely, and identify issues early. That’s why we're creating opportunities for industry partners to test, learn and share feedback as the programme develops.
What’s next
Building and inviting the DVS providers into the sandbox is one step in a wider programme of testing and collaboration.
Later this year, GDS will host a testing event with stakeholders to help us further test technical integration and collect feedback ahead of launch. More information on this will follow.
This work aims to build confidence across the whole system:
Transforming the driver experience

The Roadmap for modern digital government sets out to make life easier for people, drive growth and deliver on smarter, more efficient public services. The digital driving licence is part of this transformation, and is being achieved alongside other important product updates for drivers. This includes the GOV.UK App adding the Driver and vehicles account feature as a native feature, which is now in testing with wider release planned in a few months.
Together, these products will make it easier for people to interact with government in ways that are convenient for them, delivering on the Roadmap’s ambitions.
If you’re a registered DVS provider, register for access to the GOV.UK Wallet sandbox

title: Food Crime Update

content.content: Cymraeg

Trust in food isn’t something we can take for granted and one of the biggest threats to that trust is food crime. Sadly, there will always be individuals who are willing to risk confidence in British food for a quick profit, which is why the on-going work of the FSA’s National Food Crime Unit (NFCU) remains so essential. The past few months have shown just how active this fight continues to be.

In Dudley, a joint operation with the local council and police partners uncovered an unapproved meat cutting plant, leading to four arrests and the removal of more four tonnes of illegal meat from the food chain. In another operation, involving multiple partners including the Greater Manchester and Staffordshire Police, and Stoke-on-Trent City Council, an investigation into illegal frozen food products has resulted in one arrest and the seizure of more than 33 tonnes of suspect stock across more than a hundred businesses.

In Leicester, we worked alongside local authorities and the police to tackle the online sale of illegally prepared ‘smokies’, removing unsafe meat from circulation and making one arrest. Meanwhile, in Essex, our officers investigated suspected counterfeit wine worth more than half a million pounds.

These cases span different regions, products, and criminal methods but they share a common thread. Food crime is never victimless. It puts public health at risk, defrauds the public, and undermines the honest businesses that play by the rules. Left unchecked, food crime erodes the confidence that underpins our entire food system.

Protecting the public means staying one step ahead of those who seek to exploit the system for profit. That’s why we need to stay proactive and continue working closely with the police, local authorities, and other partners.

If you would like to keep updated about the risks from food crime and share best practice on strengthening the industry’s response to it, you can subscribe to the NFCU’s news bulletin.  You can also report food crime to Food Crime Confidential, in full confidence, at gov.uk/food-crime/report or by calling 0800 028 1180.
Katie PettiferChief Executive of FSA

title: Why post-market surveillance is a priority for the MHRA AI Airlock programme

content.content: It is widely recognised that AI technologies have the potential to positively transform healthcare by improving patient outcomes, supporting clinical decision-making and helping health services work more efficiently. However, AI systems can behave differently once they move from controlled testing environments into real-world clinical settings. The data, users, workflows and patient populations they encounter may also change over time, and these changes can affect performance.

Manufacturers of medical devices are required to monitor how their devices perform once they are in use. This is achieved through post-market surveillance (PMS), the ongoing process of collecting and reviewing information about a device's safety, performance and effectiveness throughout its lifetime. PMS helps manufacturers identify emerging issues, understand how devices are performing in real-world settings and take action where needed.

However, the importance of PMS extends beyond regulatory compliance. The National Commission into the Regulation of AI in Healthcare highlighted that AI regulation should be lifecycle-based, recognising that assurance does not end at market entry but continues throughout deployment and use. The Commission also emphasised that the safe adoption of AI is a system-wide responsibility, requiring manufacturers, healthcare organisations, professionals, regulators and others to play a role in identifying, managing and responding to risks as evidence emerges in real-world settings. Finally, as we move into a world where device performance is increasingly data sensitive and may rapidly change, proactively monitoring for and responding to emerging trends will be an important part of safe and responsible device deployment. This blog looks at what the AI Airlock has learned about applying PMS to AI-enabled medical devices, why practical challenges remain, and how the next phase of the programme will build on this work.
What earlier Airlock work told us

Over the past two years, during the pilot and Phase 2, the AI Airlock has explored PMS across a range of candidate technologies through workshops and engagement with regulatory, clinical and technical stakeholders. This work has helped the programme examine how existing PMS requirements apply to AI-enabled medical devices in practice and identify the areas where further evidence and testing are needed.
Phase 1 – FAMOS and continuous monitoring

The pilot phase first explored this challenge through Newton’s Tree’s FAMOS platform, one of the programme’s first four case studies, which examined whether continuous, near-real-time monitoring could strengthen PMS for AI-enabled medical devices. Building on the case study’s real-world testing across 2 deployment sites, a simulation workshop considered how monitoring could detect changes arising from the model, input data and interactions between users and the device, and how the earlier identification of emerging risks and performance changes might support risk management. The case study also explored monitoring measures related to data quality, performance drift and automation bias. Together, the work highlighted the potential for earlier identification of performance trends that could affect safety, while also raising practical questions about access to suitable real-world data, clinically meaningful thresholds, false alarms, stakeholder responsibilities and the action required when a signal is detected (AI Airlock Sandbox Pilot Programme Report; PMS simulation workshop report).
Phase 2: PMS and predetermined change control plans (PCCPs)

Phase 2 tested these questions further across several AI technologies. The Phase 2 findings, captured in the Programme Report, reinforced a central lesson: point-in-time, pre-market validation alone may not fully reflect how an AI medical device will perform in practice. Real-world performance can be difficult to reproduce or to address entirely or accurately in a controlled setting. That is why post-market monitoring needs to be considered early and prospectively designed as complementary to the device’s pre-market evidence, intended use and lifecycle plans.

Phase 2 also examined the relationship between PMS and predetermined change control plans (PCCPs), which describe planned modifications to software and how those modifications will be assessed, across several AI technologies, including through a dedicated simulation workshop. The work showed that managing change in AI-enabled medical devices requires a joined-up lifecycle approach: pre-market evidence should reflect the intended use, deployment environment and anticipated changes, while PMS should monitor real-world performance and identify changes that may affect safety, performance or the device’s intended purpose. The workshop also explored how manufacturers might assess whether a change is significant and whether it falls within an agreed PCCP or requires further regulatory action. Together, the findings highlighted the importance of defining monitoring measures, decision thresholds and responsibilities early, as well as proactively capturing usage and performance data post-market, while retaining sufficient flexibility to respond to evidence generated once the device is in use (AI Airlock Sandbox Phase 2 Programme Report and Insights from the AI Airlock Simulation Workshop: Post Market Surveillance and Predetermined Change Control Plans).
Why PMS remains a practical challenge

While the principles of PMS remain the same, applying them to AI medical devices can present different challenges compared with more traditional or relatively static devices. Unlike fixed devices, AI systems may be particularly sensitive to changes in input data, the clinical environment and the way people use and rely on the device, creating additional complexity when monitoring real-world performance.

The importance of PMS has also been reinforced by the National Commission into the Regulation of AI in Healthcare, which highlighted the need for stronger post-market assurance, including monitoring and the use of real-world evidence. The Commission recognised the Airlock’s findings that assurance for AI does not end at market entry, but must continue throughout the product lifecycle, with manufacturers, healthcare organisations, professionals, regulators and others all playing a role in the safe deployment and oversight of AI technologies.

Manufacturers may therefore need further support to translate existing PMS requirements into monitoring arrangements that are effective and appropriate for AI. The practical questions include what to monitor, how to set clinically meaningful thresholds, how to identify and investigate drift, how to obtain suitable real-world data, and when a detected change should trigger action.

Continuous or near-real-time monitoring may enable emerging trends to be identified earlier, but may not be appropriate in every case. The approach should be proportionate to the device, its risk and the context in which it is used, with a clear purpose for the data collected and agreed responsibilities for reviewing signals and responding to them.

Further clarity may also be needed on the respective roles of manufacturers, healthcare organisations and other actors. The aim is to provide regulatory confidence without imposing impractical monitoring arrangements or generating large volumes of data that do not support meaningful decisions.
What the next phase will explore

Building on these findings, the Airlock has selected post-market surveillance and lifecycle oversight as the first regulatory focus area for Phase 3, recognising the need for further evidence on how these approaches can be applied effectively and proportionately in practice (AI Airlock Phase 3 application).

To help shape this phase, the Airlock held a series of expert stakeholder workshops over the summer with colleagues contributing regulatory, clinical and technical perspectives. The discussions examined how PMS expectations apply to AI-enabled medical devices, including:
These discussions informed the PMS challenge areas and the questions that applicants are now invited to explore.

Supported by multi-year funding from DHSC, Phase 3 will allow the programme to move beyond annual funding cycles, be more flexible in project design and pursue more ambitious, longer-term testing. Working with innovators and stakeholders, the Airlock will explore and test practical approaches to capturing deployment-context factors more proactively; defining meaningful thresholds and proportionate actions when signals arise; maintaining effective monitoring in remote, at-home or direct-to-consumer settings with varying levels of oversight; and ensuring that the right information on safety, performance and change effectively reaches the right people at the right time.

The aim is not to predetermine a single solution or policy position, but to generate evidence about which approaches work in practice, how they can be tailored to a device, its risk and deployment context, and where existing requirements are sufficient or further guidance, tools or regulatory support may be needed. Taking this approach, the Airlock hopes to identify practical, proportionate methodologies and/or processes that support innovation while protecting patients and the public as AI-enabled medical devices are deployed across the health system.

The Phase 3 call for applications is now open and applications can be submitted on a rolling basis. We welcome proposals from AI-enabled medical device developers and manufacturers, providers of solutions to regulatory challenges, and other stakeholders who can help test practical approaches to PMS and lifecycle oversight. If your organisation could contribute to these challenge areas, find out more and apply through the AI Airlock Phase 3 application page. AI Airlock Phase 3 application - GOV.UK.

title: Historic Court Buildings: The Royal Courts of Justice, from Queen Victoria to the bear pit

content.content: Over 1,000 rooms, three and a half miles of corridors, and the biggest Victorian mosaic floor in Europe.

In this episode, we are joined by Richard from the Royal Courts of Justice Estates Office to explore the history of this iconic building, from its construction in the 1880s to its connections with Queen Victoria, who watched barristers arguing below from a balcony, in an area that became known as the 'bear garden'.
We discuss some of the building's more unusual stories, including a mysterious room number staff have never been able to fully remove, and an accident involving the clock tower.

title: Inside Defra's octopus conference

content.content: Since 2025, fishermen in south-west England have seen a sharp increase in octopus catches. While this has created new opportunities for some, others have raised concerns about impacts on shellfish fisheries. Even where the increase has brought benefits, it has meant adapting to a fishery that has looked very different from the one many fishermen have known for years.

Similar increases have been reported elsewhere in Europe over the past few years, raising questions about what is driving the change and what it could mean for the future. There is still no clear agreement on what is causing the increase in octopus numbers, how long they are here to stay, or how fisheries should respond.
Bringing people together

To explore these issues, Defra hosted a conference on 15 October bringing together fishermen, fisheries managers, international experts, and scientists. The conference provided an opportunity for people with different experiences and expertise to share what they are seeing.
Fishermen spoke about the practical impacts on their businesses and local fisheries – setting out both the opportunities and the consequences.
Scientists shared the latest scientific findings and evidence on the species, highlighted the unknowns, and set out what's planned in terms of data collection and research.

International experts shared lessons from their experiences in managing a similar octopus bloom in Brittany - and we also heard from the Marine Stewardship Council on how MSC certified fisheries in Spain and Australia are managed.
Fisheries managers explained the challenges of making decisions when there is still limited evidence.
Participants also discussed ideas for future management and identified priorities for further research.
Reflections from the conference
What did people tell us?
The clearest message from the day was that the increase in octopus numbers is being experienced differently across fisheries and locations.

For some fishermen, increased catches have created a new opportunity. For others, particularly those working in shellfish fisheries, it has added pressure to already challenging conditions and raised concerns about octopus feeding on shellfish, gear interactions, displacement and future access.
What did we learn?

The discussions also showed how much is still unknown. People were keen to better understand whether the increase in octopus numbers is likely to continue, and what, if any, action should be taken while we continue to learn more.

Hearing directly from fishermen, scientists, fisheries managers and speakers from other countries helped bring different perspectives together. It also showed the value of combining practical experience with scientific evidence.
What happens next?

The conference helped us hear different views and experiences from across the fishing industry and fisheries management. A repeated theme was the need for decisions that are evidence-based, adaptable and fair across fisheries.
We will use what we learned, alongside existing evidence and feedback, to identify where more research is needed and help guide future work on octopus in English waters.
Keep up to date

description: Defra brought fishermen, scientists and fisheries managers together to share evidence, discuss impacts and help shape future work on the octopus fishery.

title: Avoidable requisitions are falling. What’s next?
authors: Andrew Robertson, Head of Customer Policy

content.content: At a glance

In our previous blog, Avoidable requisitions continue to fall as we work together, we thanked customers, industry bodies and HM Land Registry caseworkers for helping to reduce avoidable requisitions. To recap, the number of avoidable requisitions has fallen by at least 40% since 2022, and the rate of avoidable issues per 1,000 applications has almost halved.

That progress matters. It means fewer applications are being delayed by issues that could usually have been prevented before submission, less rework for conveyancers, fewer follow-up queries for customers and a smoother process for everyone involved.

But there is still more to do. Avoidable requisitions continue to account for a significant amount of unnecessary work across the registration process. The next phase is about focusing on the issues that still occur most often and taking practical action to prevent them.
Focus checks where they will have most impact

The infographic above groups the leading avoidable requisitions into broad categories, giving an at-a-glance view of where issues arise most often. Recurring themes include missing or unclear information in forms and plans, missing identity and other supporting evidence, and incorrect fees. These are areas where small improvements in preparation and checking can make the next significant difference.

Broad categories such as “missing information” can hide several different problems. Incomplete application details, an unsigned plan and missing Stamp Duty Land Tax evidence each need a different solution. Looking at the individual reasons for requisitions gives firms a clearer basis for checks, training and quality assurance.
Our next infographic shows the leading 10 avoidable points over 2025. A requisition may contain one or more of these:

One of the most effective ways to reduce avoidable requisitions is to understand where they are happening. Many avoidable requisitions can be reduced through simple, consistent checks before submission. These checks do not need to add unnecessary complexity. They are about making sure the application, supporting evidence and any plans tell the same clear story.
The checklist below addresses the current top 10 avoidable requisition points. You can download a copy from our training hub.
Use your data to target improvement

HM Land Registry currently emails avoidable requisition data to customers every six months. We plan to make this data available through Portal, making it easier for firms to identify recurring issues and focus improvement activity.

Different firms will see different patterns. Reviewing avoidable requisition data over time can show where an internal checklist needs updating, where staff may benefit from training or where an additional quality check would prevent repeat problems. Customers can use HM Land Registry support, training and guidance to target specific issues for maximum effect.
What HM Land Registry will do
Customers’ checks are only part of the picture. We will continue to:
Keep the momentum going

Reducing avoidable requisitions is a shared responsibility. Firms can use their data to focus checks and training on the issues that affect them most. HM Land Registry will continue to improve guidance, data, support and caseworker accuracy.
Every preventable issue removed from the process saves time and helps applications progress more smoothly for conveyancers, their clients and HM Land Registry.

description: Avoidable requisitions are falling, but preventable errors still create additional work and delay. We look at the main issues that remain, what firms can do now and how HM Land Registry is supporting further improvement.
